A young woman with short wavy brown hair stands behind a Pioneer CDJ and mixer setup on an open rooftop helipad. She wears a black cropped tank top and dark jeans, with over-ear headphones resting around her neck and small tattoos visible on both forearms. Her body faces slightly left, both hands resting on the mixer surface, eyes cast downward toward the controls. A laptop sits open to her left on the booth. Two PA speakers on stands flank her on either side. The city skyline stretches behind her in warm golden haze, sun low and diffused on the horizon.
Her right hand lifts and reaches forward, fingers curling around the jog wheel of the right CDJ, spinning it slowly counterclockwise with a light wrist roll. Her left hand slides toward the crossfader, thumb nudging it a few millimeters right, then she pulls back and rests two fingers on the gain knob, rotating it with a small deliberate twist. Her head tilts slightly downward, hair falling across her cheek as she leans in closer to read the mixer display. Her weight shifts to her left hip, torso swaying subtly in a loose rhythmic pulse. She lifts her right hand and brings it up to the headphones around her neck, raising one ear cup to her right ear with a single fluid motion, pressing it close, eyes closing briefly. Her lips part slightly as she nods once, twice, locking in. She lowers the cup back down, both hands returning to the mixer. Her fingers move across the EQ knobs in a rolling sequence, high to mid to low, each turned with small precise rotations. Her body continues its slow sway, shoulders rolling forward then back. She glances briefly toward the laptop, taps a single key with her right index finger, then returns her gaze to the CDJ. The city glows behind her, warm light catching the edge of her shoulder and jaw.
Background audio is the open-air ambient rooftop environment — low wind movement, distant city hum below. Close foley includes the tactile click of CDJ jog wheel resistance, the faint mechanical tick of knob detents turning, and the soft thud of the crossfader sliding on its rail. Music bleeding from the speakers is a slow-building melodic techno track — deep rolling bass, sparse percussive hats, a distant chord pad rising and falling in long sustained waves, mood introspective and warm.

After a brief pause, another short, audible sniff is heard. The man then continues to speak, his voice maintaining the same quality, as he states, "So bad. So bad." He elaborates further, emphasizing his point with a final statement, "This got to be, it's got to be the worst tool I've ever seen."
